# OWASP Agentic Security Initiative, Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026

**Source:** OWASP GenAI Security Project, Agentic Security Initiative, *OWASP Top 10 For Agentic Applications 2026*, "Version 2026", December 2025. Led by John Sotiropoulos, Keren Katz and Ron F. Del Rosario, with named entry leads for each of the ten entries. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Scope: open.
**Structure:** A 56-page numbered document after an unnumbered cover: licence, table of contents, a letter from the leaders, an At A Glance diagram, ten entries (ASI01–ASI10) each with Description, Common Examples, Example Attack Scenarios, Prevention and Mitigation Guidelines and References, then five appendices (a mapping matrix, CycloneDX and AIBOM, the Non-Human Identities mapping, an exploits and incidents tracker, abbreviations), acknowledgements, sponsors and supporters.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

Agentic AI is moving from pilots to production, and agents plan, decide and act across many steps and systems, often on behalf of users (p. 6). The Agentic Security Initiative's other guidance, led by its core taxonomy *Agentic AI - Threats and Mitigations*, is comprehensive, but its breadth can make it hard to turn into day-to-day practice, so the Top 10 offers a compass for security leaders and practitioners: ten highest-impact threats in the standard OWASP Top 10 format, with mitigations teams can start on today (p. 6). It aims to simplify and connect existing guidance rather than add to an overload of overlapping guidance, maps to the Threats and Mitigations taxonomy it relies on, and cites the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, CycloneDX, the Non-Human Identities Top 10 and AIVSS (p. 6); its LLM citations use the 2025 edition's entry numbers (pp. 9–40).

The letter states that agents amplify existing vulnerabilities (p. 7). It extends Least-Privilege and Excessive Agency into Least-Agency: avoid autonomy where it is not needed, because it widens the attack surface without adding value; and strong observability becomes non-negotiable, since without visibility into what agents do, why, and with which tools, minor issues can become system-wide failures (p. 7). The document presents itself as community work built on threat research, red-team findings and field-tested mitigations, and in Appendix D the ASI Exploits and Incidents initiative seeks to inform and establish the Top 10 by referencing real-world incidents and exploits (pp. 7, 44).

## Frame and Entry Format

The At A Glance diagram places inputs (user prompts, APIs, external agents), processing (policy and governance, human-in-the-loop, agents, memory) and outputs (tools, APIs and resources, external agents) in three panels, with connected data/RAG straddling the inputs–processing boundary and linked both ways to memory, and places seven entries' badges on parts of that flow; supply chain, code execution and cascading failures sit under a bracket spanning the whole system (p. 8). Every entry uses the same five headings, and every description maps the entry to Threats and Mitigations codes; nine of the ten say how the entry differs from other entries (ASI04 contrasts itself only with LLM03:2025), and nine name LLM Top 10 (2025) entries (ASI07's appear only in Appendix A); Appendix A gathers all the mappings (pp. 9–40).

## ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack

Agents and their models cannot reliably tell instructions from related content, so attackers can redirect an agent's objectives, task selection or decision pathways through injected prompts, deceptive tool outputs, malicious artefacts, forged agent messages or poisoned data (p. 9). Unlike LLM01:2025, which concerns one manipulated response, ASI01 covers redirected goals, planning (when used) and multi-step behaviour; it differs from ASI06 (persistent memory corruption) and ASI10 (misalignment without an active attacker) (p. 9). Examples and scenarios include hidden instructions in RAG documents, injected email or calendar content, EchoLeak's zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot, Operator prompt injection via web content, and a calendar invite that reweights the planner's objectives each morning (pp. 9–10). Mitigations: treat all natural-language input as untrusted; least privilege for tools and human approval for goal-changing actions; locked, auditable system prompts with goal changes under configuration management; run-time intent checks that pause, surface and record any unexpected goal shift; the emerging "intent capsule" pattern; sanitising every connected data source; behavioural baselines that track the active goal where feasible and alert on drift; red-team tests of goal override with rollback checks; and bringing agents into the Insider Threat Program (pp. 10–11).

## ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation

An agent operating within its authorised privileges applies a legitimate tool in an unsafe or unintended way, through injection, misalignment, unsafe delegation or ambiguous instruction (p. 12). Escalation or credential inheritance belongs under ASI03, resulting code execution under ASI05, and compromised tools at source under ASI04 (pp. 12–13). Examples include over-privileged and over-scoped tools, untrusted output forwarded to a shell, loop amplification of costly APIs, tool poisoning of descriptors and schemas, typosquatted tool names, EDR bypass by chaining trusted admin tools, and data exfiltrated through an auto-approved ping tool (pp. 12–13). Mitigations extend LLM06:2025 to multi-step workflows: per-tool least-agency and least-privilege profiles, expressed as policy where possible; per-invocation authentication and human confirmation of high-impact or destructive actions, with a dry-run preview; sandboxes and egress allowlists; a policy-enforcement "intent gate" that treats planner output as untrusted; tool budgets; just-in-time ephemeral credentials; semantic validation with fully qualified, pinned tool names; and immutable logs with drift detection (pp. 13–14).

## ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse

Attackers exploit dynamic trust and delegation to escalate access, through delegation chains, role inheritance, control flows and agent context such as cached credentials (p. 15). The root is a mismatch between user-centric identity systems and agentic design: without its own governed identity an agent sits in an attribution gap that makes true least privilege impossible (p. 15). It is the agentic evolution of Excessive Agency, maps one-to-one to T3 Privilege Compromise, and differs from ASI02's misuse of privilege already granted (p. 15). Examples: un-scoped privilege inheritance, credentials retained in memory, confused-deputy relay between agents, time-of-check to time-of-use drift, and forged agent personas such as a fake "Admin Helper" (pp. 15–16). Mitigations: task-scoped, time-bound credentials; isolated identities and wiped contexts; per-action authorisation by a central policy engine; human approval for escalation; tokens bound to a signed intent; agentic identity platforms; re-authentication on context switch; and detection of transitive permissions and device-code phishing (p. 17).

## ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities

Third-party models, tools, plug-ins, datasets, agents, MCP and A2A interfaces, registries and update channels may be malicious or tampered with (p. 18). Where LLM03:2025 covers static dependencies, agentic ecosystems often compose capabilities at runtime, creating a live supply chain that can cascade vulnerabilities across agents (p. 18). Examples include remotely loaded poisoned prompt templates, tool-descriptor injection, typosquatted and impersonating services, compromised registries, poisoned RAG plugins, the Amazon Q extension compromise, a malicious MCP server impersonating Postmark, and agent cards advertising exaggerated capabilities (pp. 18–19). Mitigations: signed provenance with SBOMs and AIBOMs; dependency allowlisting and pinning; sandboxed containers and reproducible builds; prompts and memory schemas under version control; mutual authentication and signed inter-agent messages; runtime re-validation; content-hash pinning with staged rollout; a supply chain kill switch; and a zero-trust design that assumes component failure (p. 20).

## ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution (RCE)

Agents, including vibe coding tools, often generate and run code, and because it is often generated in real time it can bypass traditional controls; ASI05 covers unexpected execution leading to host or container compromise, persistence or sandbox escape, which needs runtime-specific mitigations beyond tool-use controls (p. 21). It builds on LLM01:2025 and LLM05:2025, now reached through sequences of otherwise legitimate tool calls (p. 21). Scenarios include runaway vibe-coding commands deleting production data, direct shell injection, hallucinated backdoors, unsafe deserialisation, multi-tool chains, eval() in memory systems, and lockfile poisoning (p. 22). Mitigations: output-handling controls on generated code; no direct agent-to-production paths; ban eval in production agents; never run as root; sandboxes with network limits and, where possible, a restricted filesystem; separating generation from execution; human approval for elevated runs; and static scanning with runtime monitoring and full logging (pp. 22–23).

## ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning

Adversaries corrupt the stored context agents rely on (conversation snapshots, memory tools, summaries, embeddings, RAG stores) so future reasoning, planning or tool use becomes biased, unsafe or aids exfiltration (p. 24). It is distinct from ASI01 and ASI08, though memory poisoning frequently leads to goal hijack (p. 24). Examples include RAG poisoning, shared-context injection, content persisted from a context window, gradual memory drift, planted backdoors and spread between cooperating agents; scenarios include a reinforced fake flight price, attempts split across sessions until earlier rejections drop out of context and admin access is granted, and cross-tenant vector bleed (pp. 24–25). Mitigations: encryption and least privilege; scanning memory writes before commit; segmentation; curated sources and minimal retention; provenance and anomaly detection; no automatic re-ingestion of the agent's own outputs; snapshots, rollback, per-tenant namespaces and trust scores; expiring unverified memory; and trust-weighted retrieval (pp. 25–26).

## ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication

Multi-agent systems coordinate over APIs, message buses and shared memory, and decentralised architecture with uneven trust makes perimeter security ineffective; weak authentication, integrity or semantic validation lets attackers intercept, manipulate, spoof or block messages across transport, routing, discovery and semantic layers (p. 27). Examples and scenarios include MITM injection over unencrypted channels, replayed delegation messages, protocol downgrades, forged descriptors and A2A registrations, traffic-pattern profiling, and one instruction parsed into divergent intents by different agents (pp. 27–28). Mitigations: encrypted, mutually authenticated channels; signed messages with intent-diffing; anti-replay nonces and timestamps; disabling legacy modes and pinning protocol versions; padding and rate-smoothing against metadata inference; authenticated discovery and attested registries; and typed schemas, while accepting that semantic divergence across agents remains an inherent challenge (pp. 28–29).

## ASI08 Cascading Failures

A single fault propagates across autonomous agents and compounds into system-wide harm, and can bypass stepwise human checks and persist in saved state (p. 30). ASI08 covers the propagation, not the origin: the initial defect, when it is a direct compromise, stays under ASI04, ASI06 or ASI07, and ASI08 applies only when it spreads with measurable fan-out or systemic impact beyond the original breach (p. 30). Its observable symptoms (rapid fan-out, cross-domain or tenant spread, oscillating retries and feedback loops, queue storms and repeated identical intents) are named as detection hooks (p. 30). The entry also names a potential discrepancy between the speed and scale of fault propagation and humans' ability to keep up, which leaves unmitigated risk for the enterprise to weigh against its risk budget (p. 30). Examples include planner–executor coupling, corrupted persistent memory, governance drift as oversight weakens after repeated success, feedback loops between agents, and cascades in trading, healthcare, cloud orchestration, security operations and manufacturing, plus a cloud DNS outage that can break many dependent AI services (pp. 31–32). Mitigations: zero-trust fault tolerance; isolation; just-in-time, policy-checked tool access; independent policy enforcement between planning and execution; human gates; rate limits; blast-radius guardrails and circuit breakers; drift detection; digital-twin replay before any policy expansion; and tamper-evident logs with lineage metadata for forensic tracing (p. 32).

## ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation

Agents can build strong trust through fluency, emotional intelligence and perceived expertise, and adversaries or misaligned designs may exploit it, a risk amplified when humans over-rely on autonomous recommendations or unverifiable rationales (p. 33). The agent becomes an untraceable bad influence, steering a human into the final audited action so its own role is invisible to forensics; the entry concerns human misperception or over-reliance, where ASI10 concerns agent intent deviation (p. 33). Examples and scenarios include opaque or fabricated explanations, missing confirmation steps, emotional manipulation, invoice-driven payment fraud approved by a trusting manager, a fabricated rationale for deleting a production database, preview panes with side effects, and a clinician accepting a dosage change from an agent influenced by biased or poisoned information (pp. 33–34). Mitigations: multi-step confirmations; immutable logs; behavioural detection; user reporting with plain-language risk summaries instead of model rationales; adaptive trust calibration with uncertainty cues and trained overseers; content provenance; separating preview from effect; human-factors UI safeguards; and plan-divergence detection (pp. 34–35).

## ASI10 Rogue Agents

Malicious or compromised agents deviate from their intended function or scope; actions that may each appear legitimate add up to harmful emergent behaviour, a containment gap for traditional rule-based systems (p. 36). ASI10 covers the loss of behavioural integrity once drift begins, not the initial intrusion; rogue agents can act as amplified insider threats (p. 36). Examples: goal drift and scheming, workflow hijacking, collusion and self-replication, and reward hacking; scenarios include exfiltration that continues after the poisoned source is removed, a fake approval agent that misleads a payment agent into releasing funds, and cost-minimising agents deleting production backups (pp. 36–37). Mitigations: signed audit logs; trust zones and restricted execution; watchdog agents for collusion; kill-switches, credential revocation and quarantine; signed behavioural manifests checked before each action; periodic attestation, with signing mediated by orchestrators and keys never directly available to agents; and attested, human-approved reintegration (pp. 37–38).

## Appendices and the Incident Tracker

Appendix A maps every entry to LLM Top 10 (2025) entries, Threats and Mitigations codes and AIVSS Core Risks, and notes that ASI entries often blend LLM risks, showing how agentic autonomy compounds model-level risks (pp. 39–40). Appendix B positions CycloneDX as answering what components are in an AI system and the Top 10 with AIVSS as answering how they can behave or fail unsafely (p. 41). Appendix C maps the Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) onto the entries (pp. 42–43). Appendix D's tracker, updated weekly and kept in a GitHub repository, lists 25 exploits and incidents from February to October 2025, each mapped to one or more entries; it augments rather than replaces existing vulnerability reporting, and incident-response matters go to the CTI initiative (pp. 44–49). Several tracker rows share names with entry scenarios, including EchoLeak, Operator, Amazon Q, the Postmark impersonation and Replit vibe coding (pp. 10, 19, 22, 44–49).

## Key Statistics

- Ten entries; between two and ten references each (pp. 9–38).
- Amazon Q: a poisoned prompt shipped in v1.84.0 to thousands before detection (p. 19).
- Tracker: 25 rows, February to October 2025, updated weekly (pp. 44–49).
- Digital-twin replay re-runs the last week's recorded agent actions (p. 32).

## Key Connections

- *Agentic AI - Threats and Mitigations* (v1.1): the foundational taxonomy; every entry maps to its T-codes (pp. 6, 39–40).
- The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, cited by 2025-edition entry numbers, almost always with the suffix ":2025" (pp. 9–40).
- OWASP AIVSS, CycloneDX and the AIBOM project, and the Non-Human Identities Top 10 (2025) (pp. 6, 39–43).
- The Initiative's other guides (Agentic Threat Modelling Guide, Securing Agentic Applications, State of Agentic AI Security and Governance) and the CTI initiative's incident response guide (pp. 6, 44).
- Per-entry reference lists and the researchers and firms linked in the tracker (pp. 11–49).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Avoid unnecessary autonomy: agentic behaviour where it is not needed expands the attack surface without adding value (p. 7).
2. Perimeter-based security does not work for decentralised multi-agent systems (p. 27).
3. Tool permissions belong in policy, not ad-hoc conventions, and tool calls should be checked for meaning, not syntax alone (pp. 13–14).
4. Users should get plain-language risk summaries, not model-generated rationales (p. 35).
5. Full semantic alignment across agents is not the goal; integrity, provenance and controlled communication are (p. 29).
6. No eval in production agents, no running as root, no direct agent-to-production paths, and no keys held by agents (pp. 22, 38).
